# Distribution {#sec-distribution}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
A visual summary of your data
:::

There two entry points to think of a distribution. The first one is from the theoretical perspective, thinking about normal/gaussian or like binomial or Poission distribution. That perspective will be addressed later in this book, when we talk about statistical inference.

The second one is from a data-driven perspective. Assume for now that it is qualitative variable (@sec-qualitative-variable). That is, imagine assess the gender of all (n) pupils in a classrom (more generally a variable @sec-variable from a population @sec-population). That is mostly a sequence of male female. A distribution is a first entry point to summarizing your data. Yes, it is a summary because we are computing new numbers from the original data.

So what are the new numbers: essentially you count the number in each category. The sequence of male and female becomes a table


|      |        |
|------|--------|
| male | female |
|$n_m$ | $n_f$  |

: The number version of a distribution where $n = n_f + n_m$.

A distribution is a figure representing the data, the figure is simply two bars of different height.

Sorry if this is so obvious and boring...but what happens variable is quantitative (@sec-quantiative-variable)? How one constructs the data and the figure distribution? Imagine you measured the height of the same pupils aboave, you have a sequence of n numbers. It count based on unique value, it is quite likely that table above becomes a long column and the number in the second row is mostly one. The figure is just a plot with bar of the same height "random" spacing. Not very informative in general.

Ironically, to visualize such sequence is to convert the quantitative values into an ordinal qualitative. Think about altitude into categories: the number of columns becomes manageable, and the second row is more just 1. The key point is that these categories are arbitary, and depending on the category, one will get different distribution, because your table is different. E.g. if grade is between 0 and 20, we can create 2 catergories \[0,10) (excluding 10) and \[10, 20\], or you can divide into 4 groups or equal dist \[0,5), \[5,10), \[10,15) or even \[0,5\] and \[6, 20\]. One has to explain the reason behind these choice.

The take-home is that variable is a sequence of number, the distribution summarize/transform it into pair of discrete bin-and the number of that fall belong to that bin which is then plotted for visualization (@sec-function_viz). You can then see which value is most or least frequent, but also the frequency of all other values.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

Textbook Source Book: The Practice of Statistics (6th Edition, 2018) Authors: Daren S. Starnes and Josh Tabor Publisher: W. H. Freeman / Bedford, Freeman & Worth

The Definition In Chapter 1 ("Data Analysis"), Starnes and Tabor provide the standard, universally taught definition for the distribution of an observed variable: "The distribution of a variable tells us what values the variable takes and how often it takes these values. The distribution of a categorical variable lists the categories and gives either the count or the percent of individuals who fall in each category. The distribution of a quantitative variable tells us what values the variable takes and how often it takes those values."

We will omit the formal mathematical definition of distribution, the theoretical perspective above and  will return to that in due time.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

We omit the raw data and the table here. The first row are based on qualitative variable. For nominal variables we can change the order of the values in the x-axis (column 2 and 3).

```{r}
df_sex <- data.frame(
    sex = c("male", "female"),
    value = c(13, 16)
)

fig_sex <- ggplot(df_sex, aes(x = sex, y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()

df_lemur <- data.frame(
    species = c("indri", "catta", "mouse"),
    value = c(10, 20, 300)
)

fig_lemur_a <- ggplot(df_lemur, aes(x = species, y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()

fig_qual <- fig_sex + fig_lemur_a +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")

fig_qual
```

The first column is for a pure discrete variable, where are the second and third are for continuous with two different binning.

```{r}

# Quantitative
set.seed(1)
df_discrete <- data.frame(
    size = rpois(100, 5)) |>
    count(size)


fig_discrete <- ggplot(df_discrete, aes(x = size, xend = size, y = 0, yend = n)) +
 geom_point(aes(x = size, y = n)) +
  geom_segment() +
  theme_bw()

set.seed(1)
df_quant <- data.frame(
    size = rnorm(100, 10, 1)
)

fig_quant_a <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant_b <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant <- fig_discrete + fig_quant_a + fig_quant_b +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")
fig_quant
```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}

- The distribution is the fundamental concept, whether it is theory or appplied/data driven. A variable is a map with its distribution, it has similarites as function and figure (@sec-function_viz). Except that two variables can have teh same distribution.

- Barchart vs. histogram: the former is used with qualitative variable, the second one is used with quantitative. Mostly because and define the binning.

- For bar chart one can reoder the values on x-axis for qualitative variable (unless it is an ordinal variable). The standard is to put them from the least frequent to the most frequent (or inversely). Generally eases the interpretation

```{r}
fig_lemur_a <- ggplot(df_lemur, aes(x = species, y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()

fig_lemur_b <- ggplot(df_lemur, aes(x = reorder(species, value), y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()


fig_qual_reorder <-  fig_lemur_a + fig_lemur_b +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")

fig_qual_reorder
```

- It is possible to scale the value on the y-axis by showing the absolute count, relative count, or for quantitative variable is density so that the area under the curve equals to one. More a matter of interpreration. For instance if sample size is different and one wants to compare two distribution, frequency might be better.

```{r}
fig_quant_dens <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size, after_stat(density))) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant_freq <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size, after_stat(ncount))) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_y <- fig_quant_a  + fig_quant_freq + fig_quant_dens
fig_y
```

- A distribution summarize the raw data, thus having the distribution does not allow you to recover the raw data...
- Looking at figure is more informative, to paraphrase: A figure is worth a thousand words, a distribution is worth a million values.
- Some data-driven distribution can also be represented by smooth curve (think about the bell-shaped curve). This representation requires additional machinery. While informative and can be aestethically pleasing,  misused can be misleading.

1. The Rigorous Mathematical Statistics Definition
In theoretical statistics, when we talk about the distribution of a variable, we are referring to a Probability Distribution, which is formalized as a function (like a Cumulative Distribution Function, or CDF).

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), the authors define the distribution of a random variable X by its cumulative distribution function FX(x), which rigorously maps out the entire probability behavior of that variable:
"Let X be a random variable. The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of X, denoted by FX(x), is defined by

FX (x)=P(X≤x)

for all real numbers x. [...] The cdf completely determines the probability distribution of the random variable X."


Under this mathematical framework:

If the variable is discrete, its distribution is rigorously defined by a Probability Mass Function (PMF): p(x)=P(X=x).

If the variable is continuous, its distribution is rigorously defined by a Probability Density Function (PDF), f(x), such that P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab f(x)dx.

3. The Measure-Theoretic Definition
For advanced graduate-level mathematical statistics, a distribution is rigorously defined as a "probability measure" induced by the variable on a measurable space.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics (2nd Edition, 2003)
Author: Jun Shao
Publisher: Springer Science & Business Media

The Definition
In Chapter 1, Shao strips away the informal language entirely, defining the distribution of a variable (X) as a mathematically bound probability law:

"Let X be a random variable defined on a probability space (Ω,F,P). The distribution of X is defined as the probability measure P
X on (R,B) induced by X, i.e.,

P X (B)=P(X−1(B)) = P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}) for any Borel set B∈B."

Summary: What does a "Distribution" encompass?
No matter the tier of the textbook, a distribution must provide two essential components for a variable:

The Values: Every possible value (or range of values) that the variable can mathematically achieve.

The Frequency/Probability: The likelihood, proportion, or exact frequency with which those values occur.

Visually and analytically, we evaluate the distribution of a variable by looking at its shape (e.g., symmetric, skewed, bell-shaped), its center (e.g., mean, median), and its spread (e.g., variance, standard deviation). -->

In statistics, a distribution (or the distribution of a variable) is a foundational concept that bridges raw data with mathematical probability. Depending on whether you look at an applied context (real data) or a theoretical context (probability models), it is defined either as a summary of observed frequencies or as a mathematical function mapping probabilities to values.
Here are the rigorous definitions from three authoritative textbooks representing these different levels of statistical analysis.

1. The Applied / Data-Centric Definition
In applied and introductory statistics, the distribution of a variable is defined as a description of what values the variable takes and how often it takes them. -->
